segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and dignity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who wants all people to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, himself a human being, Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony given at the proper time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this I was appointed a herald and an apostle—I am telling the truth; I am not lying—a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I want the men in every place to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Likewise, I want women to adorn themselves in respectable attire, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or expensive clothing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but, as is fitting for women who profess reverence for God, with good works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A woman is to learn in quietness, in all submission.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to be in quietness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Adam was formed first, then Eve;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and fell into transgression.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she will be saved through childbearing, if they remain in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

notes.note: The Greek word here is the general term for a human being, not the word for a male, and it repeats the word just used for “human beings.” The point is that the mediator shares the nature of those he represents. The traditional “the man Christ Jesus” is not wrong, but it hides the echo and can be heard as a statement about maleness.

notes.phrase: the testimony given at the proper time
notes.traditional: to be testified in due time
notes.note: The Greek is very compressed, literally “the testimony in its own times,” and “given” is supplied. Most interpreters take it to mean that Christ’s self-giving is itself the witness to God’s saving purpose, borne at the time God appointed. It can also be read as pointing forward to the message that the writer was appointed to proclaim (verse 7).

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations”; in Jewish usage the plural names the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the same word “nations” where peoples as such are in view and “Gentiles” where, as here, the contrast with Israel is the point.

Standing with hands raised and palms open was the ordinary posture of prayer among both Jews and Greeks. The emphasis falls not on the gesture, which is assumed, but on the hands being “holy” and the prayer being free of anger.

The word can mean inner reasoning or doubt, or an outward dispute. Paired with “anger” and addressed to men praying together, it is usually taken as disputing, and that reading is followed here. Older versions have “doubting,” which remains possible.

notes.phrase: braided hair and gold or pearls
notes.traditional: braided hair, or gold, or pearls
notes.note: Elaborate hairstyles interwoven with gold and jewels were a conspicuous display of wealth among well-to-do women of the period, and Greek and Roman moralists made similar criticisms. The concern is ostentation in the assembly, not braiding as such.

Older versions have “silence.” The word more often describes a calm, settled, undisruptive manner than the absence of speech; its adjective is used in verse 2 for the “quiet” life believers hope to lead. Many modern translations accordingly have “quietly” or “quietness,” though some scholars still argue for “silence” here.

notes.traditional: usurp authority over; have authority over
notes.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament and is rare in Greek of the period, so its exact force is disputed. Some scholars take it neutrally (“have” or “exercise authority”), others negatively (“domineer over”) or as “assume authority” on one’s own initiative. The evidence does not settle the question; the rendering here follows the neutral reading found in most modern translations.

The Greek words for “woman” and “man” are also the ordinary words for “wife” and “husband,” and the appeal to Adam and Eve that follows concerns a married pair. Most translations take verses 8–15 to be about men and women in the gathered community; a minority of scholars read verses 11–15 as concerning wives and husbands.

This is one of the most debated phrases in the letter. The Greek has the article (“the childbearing”), and the main proposals are: saved through the role of bearing and raising children; brought safely through childbirth; or saved through the birth of the child, meaning the Messiah born of a woman. The rendering here leaves the phrase as open as the Greek does.

The Greek shifts without explanation from the singular “she will be saved” to the plural “they remain.” “She” most naturally picks up “the woman” of verse 14, Eve as representing women, and “they” is usually taken as women generally. Others suggest it means the woman and her husband, or her children.

candidates.reason: Frequent in the Pastoral Letters and 2 Peter; translators vary between “godliness,” “piety,” “devotion,” and “reverence,” and it needs to stay distinct from θεοσέβεια (v. 10).

The σωφρ- word group recurs across the Pastorals and elsewhere, with renderings ranging over “self-control,” “good sense,” “moderation,” and “propriety”; it also needs to stay distinct from ἐγκράτεια.
The choice between “quietness” and “silence” here, in Acts 22:2, and in 2 Thessalonians 3:12 (with ἡσύχιος in v. 2 and 1 Peter 3:4) is interpretively weighty and should be uniform.
With σεμνός it recurs in the Pastorals and Philippians 4:8, and is variously rendered “dignity,” “holiness,” “seriousness,” or “respectability.”
It recurs across Paul’s letters, Hebrews, and 2 Peter; translators differ on whether to distinguish it from γνῶσις (“full knowledge,” “recognition”) or to render both as “knowledge.”
